Alison: Hello, yes, I can hear you fine. I'm Alison. Sorry, I'm still getting used to all this.
Tomasz: No, it's fine, it's fine. Listen, that puzzle at the start, did you finish it? I think I was fast, I don't know.
Alison: Oh, erm, I sort of finished it. I wasn't very quick. I kept double-checking. That's me all over really.
Tomasz: Ha. I don't check, I just go. So what do you do, Alison?
Alison: I'm a practice nurse, at a GP surgery in Ipswich. So diabetes reviews, asthma, smears, jabs, that sort of thing.
Tomasz: Nurse, okay. My wife, Agnieszka, she's care assistant, in a home, residential. Shifts, nights, everything. Hard job, you know? Paid nothing.
Alison: Oh, it is hard, that's ever so hard work. I was a healthcare assistant at the hospital before I trained, so I know. Bless her. Does she like it?
Tomasz: She likes the old people. She doesn't like the managers. Same like me, I think.
Alison: (laughs) What do you do, then?

You ring a kebab shop at lunchtime, the guy swears at you, puts phone down, you ring the next one. Last month our team hit target and honestly, I carried them. I was top three on the board most of the month.
Alison: Gosh. I don't think I could do that. I'd be apologising to everyone.
Tomasz: That's why you are nurse and I am sales, yeah?
Alison: That's true. Do people really swear at you?
Tomasz: Every day. Doesn't bother me. It's not personal, they don't know me. You just keep going.
Alison: I suppose that's a good attitude to have, really. I take everything home with me, I'm afraid. I'll lie awake thinking, did I put the right code in.
Tomasz: No, no. Home is home. You are Ipswich, yeah? I've never been. For me it's Birmingham Airport, M6, that's my life. Junction 10 is a nightmare every morning.
Alison: Oh, I've heard about the M6. Ipswich is all right, it's quiet. I walk along the river most days. And I've got a cat, Biscuit. You might have seen his tail in my picture.
Tomasz: I saw a bit of orange, yeah. Not a cat man. Dog, maybe. My son wants a dog. He's fifteen, he'll never walk it, he's on PlayStation whole day.
Alison: (laughs) They all are. My son was the same at fifteen, and now he's got a little girl of his own, so it all comes round. I mind her on Fridays.
Tomasz: That's nice. Grandmother, yeah? You don't look it.
Alison: Oh, stop it. I'm fifty-nine. I'm ever so proud of her, though.
Tomasz: And apart from work? You walk, you have cat...
Alison: I sing in a choir, alto. Tuesday nights in a church hall. We're doing the Christmas concert soon, so it's all carols at the minute.
Tomasz: Choir. Okay. I do five-a-side, Thursday. Same idea, you know. You go with people, you shout a bit.
Alison: Well, we try not to shout! But I suppose, yes, it's sort of the same. It's for the company really.
Tomasz: Exactly. Company. And beer after, for us. For you I think tea and biscuit.
Alison: Tea and biscuits, yes, and I'm meant to be cutting down, so that's going well.
Tomasz: Ha. Listen, Ipswich Town, you follow? They went up, yeah? Very good.
Alison: My dad was a season ticket holder, so I keep half an eye. I was chuffed, I must say. Do you have a team?

Hetal: Yes, I made this kurti. The embroidery also, by hand. Sorry, it's very simple.

Hetal: Oh, you are from Ghana?
Abena: Accra, originally. I've been here a long time now. And you?

Abena: Oh, it is. My mother still has —

Alison: Colchester, with his partner. They've got a little girl now, I mind her on Fridays.

calls.C0041:

Abena: Oh?
Karen: Saturdays. They'll say, yeah, I'll be in, and then half eight, text. Every week. I end up doing the till and the back room on my own.

Abena: Erm, I'll be honest, for me it's mostly the people and the singing. I'm not sure how devout I am.
Karen: Same, sort of. Routine, and the people. Though, I dunno. It matters a bit more than I let on, I think.
Abena: That's honest. I think that's true of a lot of us.
Karen: What's the singing like, then? Bet it's better than ours.
Abena: Well, it's loud. There's drumming. You'd —
calls.C0042:
Tomasz: Hello, mate! Tomasz, Walsall. You're Darren, yeah?
Darren: Alright, yeah, Darren. Bridgwater, Somerset.
Tomasz: Somerset, okay, cider, farms. What do you do?

Tomasz: No, you tell them. I tell my manager the training is rubbish, in the meeting. Two warnings. (laughs) But I'm right.

Tomasz: Okay, maybe you are cleverer than me. What you drive?

Tomasz: That's good, mate. Really. I'm renting, eight years. Landlord, boiler, three weeks to fix. Football, you watch?
Darren: Bristol City, from a distance. Radio and the app mostly.
Tomasz: Wolves for me, and Lech Poznań from Poland. You bet?
Darren: Not really, the odd one at the Grand National.
Tomasz: Listen, accumulators, Saturday, five teams. Last week four came in, one let me down. The referee, honestly, Wolves game, he gave a penalty —
calls.C0043:

Hetal: Me also! I want a little website one day, for the blouses. But now, erm, I just want regular money.

Hetal: Oh, I'm sorry.
Karen: It's alright. I still have the radio on in summer, for the cricket. Sort of keeps him about, you know.

Karen: No, you're alright. Do you watch the Sewing Bee?

calls.C0044:
Alison: Hello, can you hear me all right? I'm Alison.
Abena: Yes, perfectly. I'm Abena. Hello.

Abena: (laughs) Well, I try. Thank you. Some of those vases I bought from a potter in Accra. Where are you?

calls.C0046:
Darren: Alright? Darren. Can you hear me?

calls.C0047:

calls.C0048:
